transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-20
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Myers (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Head of Platform, NexaCare), Sofia Martinez (SRE), Ethan Wu (CTO)

Auto-generated summary (brief):
NexaCare is evaluating Redwood's Console for end-to-end request forensics: request traces, KV cache mismatch diagnostics, error analysis and fallbacks during degraded model availability. Customer wants a runbook for triage and to validate latency guarantees for conversational assistants in production.

Topics covered:
- Walkthrough of Console request trace UI and correlation with logs
- KV cache hit/miss diagnostics and cache invalidation scenarios
- Error classification: soft vs hard failures, partial responses, and graceful fallback to smaller model variants
- Replay and trace playback for reproducing bad responses
- Security and data residency notes (quick)

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Jordan: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Jordan from Redwood, uh we have Priya with me, SE, and we're excited to walk through the request sleuthing and the runtime playbook. how's everyone doing?
[00:00:12] Liam: Doing good, thanks. Big reason we're here is we've seen some intermittent latency spikes and a few odd hallucinations from the assistant in prod last week, so we want to understand how we'd triage that end to end.
[00:00:25] Priya: yeah totally. quick agenda: show the request inspector, trace correlation with logs, demo a KV-cache mismatch scenario, and then play through fallback policies. we'll surface what you should collect for an RCA. sound good?
[00:00:36] Sofia: perfect. our SREs are mostly on k8s and we have a caching layer in front of the model runner; we suspect the kv cache maybe is getting out of sync after recent rolling updates.
[00:00:47] Ethan: and from infra perspective we want to know if Redwood Dedicated or Private would make this easier, like can we avoid the cache inconsistency entirely?
[00:00:55] Priya: quick note — cache inconsistency can come from either prefix eviction or model variant mismatch; we'll demo both. the Console has a filter to surface any request where the key-version in the trace doesn't match the runtime's active model fingerprint.
[00:01:10] Jordan: alright, we'll jump into the Console. Priya do you want to share your screen?
[00:01:15] Priya: yep sharing now. give me a sec.
[00:01:40] [screen share visible] Priya: okay this is the Requests page — you can search by request id, user id, model name, or error code. here's a sample failing request from your example dataset, id ends 7fac.
[00:01:55] Priya: on the right is the trace timeline — you can expand each span. notice at t+120ms there's a 'kv_cache.lookup' with a miss, then at t+450ms we call into the runtime and there's a kernel selection path 'quant-ops-v2' and afterwards we see an unusually long compile step, which is often the culprit for warmup slowness.
[00:02:20] Sofia: hmm compile step — but we pinned model versions in our last deploy, shouldn't we avoid compile?
[00:02:28] Priya: good question. sometimes small changes in hardware or quantization flags trigger a recompile path; also if the model shard got rescheduled to a different GPU type the kernel selector might prefer a different kernel, which shows up as a compile span.
[00:02:42] Liam: that matches the timeframe of our infra autoscaler churning nodes at 01:00 UTC.
[00:02:50] Priya: exactly. Console shows a diff view: pre- and post-deploy active kernel fingerprints. you can diff traces side-by-side to see the time delta.
[00:03:10] [00:03:10] Priya: next, KV cache mismatch demo — I'm going to force a scenario where the cache key version is stale and the runtime falls back to recompute full attention.
[00:03:20] Priya: running the synthetic payload now... you should see a cache-mismatch flag in the trace properties and an automatic annotation suggesting "invalidate-prefix" or "bust-kv-key".
[00:03:34] Sofia: is the annotation auto-generated or manual?
[00:03:36] Priya: it's heuristics based — we look for a set of conditions: miss rate spike, cache key version mismatch, and repeated recompute for same user prefix within a short window. then we surface the most likely remediation.
[00:03:50] Ethan: the heuristic sounds useful but will we get false positives?
[00:03:53] Priya: sometimes, yeah. that's why we show a confidence score and links to raw spans so your SRE can validate.
[00:04:05] [screen shows a replay button] Priya: here's the trace playback. it replays token-level timings, and you can step through the KV operations and runtime kernels. you can also export the trace as a zip which includes the span logs, the raw request, and the model fingerprint metadata.
[00:04:22] Liam: can we ingest those zips into our internal postmortem system?
[00:04:26] Priya: yes — the export is a small tar.gz with JSON spans; we can provide a mapping doc for your engineers to parse.
[00:04:34] Jordan: quick pause — security: payloads are redacted by default in hosted mode for exports; in Private deployments you control retention and export policies.
[00:04:46] Sofia: good. on the redaction, do we get deterministic hashes for user ids so we can correlate across traces without exposing PII?
[00:04:55] Priya: yes, Console supports salted deterministic hashing with a customer-managed salt in Private mode; for hosted we use a Redwood-managed salt but you can request deterministic mapping under enterprise contracts.
[00:05:06] [00:05:06] Priya: back to fallbacks — here's a trace where the runtime timed out on the large model and the router fell back to a smaller quantized variant. notice the trace shows the routing decision and the fallback latency added ~80ms but preserved a coherent response.
[00:05:24] Ethan: do we get metrics on success rate of fallbacks? like how often the smaller model returns acceptable quality?
[00:05:30] Priya: yes, Optimize ties into this: we can surface BLEU-like or semantic-similarity metrics on your golden prompts and show quality delta per variant. we can also set automated rollback if quality drops below threshold during a rollout.
[00:05:44] Liam: that would help for canarying.
[00:05:48] [00:05:48] Priya: next, error classification. Console tags spans as soft errors (partial output, truncated token stream), hard errors (runtime crash, OOM), and infra errors (network, storage). here's an example of a soft error where the decoder emitted a stop token prematurely; the transcript shows the partial output and we link to the user prompt and the first tokens of the model response.
[00:06:10] Sofia: is there a way to group these errors automatically? we have thousands of requests per minute.
[00:06:15] Priya: yep, we have clustering — you can create alerts on signatures (e.g., "premature-stop + model:x"), and Console will surface a top-N stack with example traces.
[00:06:26] Jordan: and alerts can be routed to Slack or PagerDuty with the trace link.
[00:06:31] Liam: nice. about replay — if we replay traces for offline debugging, does that hit production models?
[00:06:37] Priya: replay can be sandboxed. by default we replay against a sandboxed model snapshot in Redwood Dedicated/Private or an isolated runtime so you don't impact prod. we also support replay against a local docker runner for your engineers.
[00:06:50] Ethan: can we do A/B replay, like compare two model builds side-by-side?
[00:06:54] Priya: yes, the replay UI supports parallel runs and diffing token timelines. it's how we validate whether a change regresses latency or quality.
[00:07:05] [00:07:05] Sofia: earlier you mentioned kernel selection — can we pin kernels to avoid compile-induced latency?
[00:07:12] Priya: in Dedicated and Private you can pin kernel profiles per model build; for hosted we have a kernel cache and warmup options but sometimes there's a brief compile cost on the first N requests.
[00:07:24] Liam: so for our use case where 99th p95 latency matters, Dedicated might be better?
[00:07:29] Jordan: typically yes. Dedicated reduces variability, plus you get reserved GPU pools and more control on autoscaling churn.
[00:07:35] Ethan: what's the onboarding timeline for a Dedicated pilot? we have compliance review windows.
[00:07:39] Jordan: usually 4–6 weeks for pilot — includes provisioning, a short bench run, and onboarding with one of our solutions engineers. we'll tee up a draft SOW.
[00:07:47] [00:07:47] Priya: demoing one more thing — the "request heatmap" for a given user session. you can see token-time distribution and where latency is spent: prefix KV, kernel compute, or RPC to external tools.
[00:07:58] Priya: here's a real world example: a spike where multiple requests for same user showed repeated recompute because prefix entries were evicted after a TTL bug. the Console flagged a TTL anomaly and recommended increasing the prefix TTL for that app route.
[00:08:14] Sofia: can TTL be per-route? we have some routes that are ephemeral and some that are long-lived.
[00:08:18] Priya: yes, TTL is configurable per route and you can override via the SDK. Optimize can also suggest route-specific TTLs based on observed session lengths.
[00:08:30] Liam: from an instrumentation standpoint what do we need to send? our current tracing has request-id and user-id but not token-level timings.
[00:08:37] Priya: minimal is request-id, model name, and a timestamped sequence of events. we can ingest various trace formats (OTel, honeycomb-ish spans) or you can use Redwood's lightweight agent that emits token-level spans.
[00:08:50] Ethan: retention — how long are traces kept and can we set custom retention?
[00:08:55] Priya: hosted defaults to 30 days, enterprise plans can go to 90+ or be configured to ship raw exports to your S3 in near-real-time. Private you control retention.
[00:09:06] [00:09:06] Jordan: quick objection we often hear: "we don't want extra cost from capturing token-level spans." in most cases the additional storage is minor versus value in fast RCA; also Optimize helps you sample intelligently — e.g., preserve all error traces but sample success traces.
[00:09:21] Sofia: that sampling is important.
[00:09:24] [00:09:24] Priya: wrapping up — typical runbook steps we recommend for NexaCare: 1) collect trace+export 2) diff pre/post deploy kernel fingerprints 3) check kv_cache key-version in spans 4) run replay in sandbox 5) if fallback triggered, check quality delta and consider route-specific TTL/kvs tweaks.
[00:09:45] Liam: good checklist. any quick notes on SSO and audit logs?
[00:09:50] Jordan: Console supports SAML SSO and per-role RBAC; audit logs track trace exports, SSO logins, and config changes. enterprise also gets longer audit retention.
[00:09:59] Ethan: ok next steps we talked about earlier — provide the sample trace, get the SOW and pricing, and draft the KV-cache annotated runbook.
[00:10:07] Priya: I'll compile the annotated runbook and share screen recording clip of the KV-mismatch demo.
[00:10:12] Jordan: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with dates.
[00:10:16] Liam: thanks all — appreciated the straight answers.

End of call notes:
- Short demo captured several concrete triage levers: kernel pinning, per-route TTLs, prioritized trace exports, and sandboxed replay.
- Customer is leaning towards a Dedicated pilot to reduce 99th percentile variability; Redwood to send pilot SOW and pricing.
- Customer to provide sample trace bundle.
